# Question Key

1. Mitosis evolved before meiosis. What two specific molecular or structural changes to standard mitotic cell division had to occur for the eukaryotic ancestor to achieve meiotic reduction division (2n to n)?

<text style="background-color:lightcyan">
First, the pairing and synapsis of homologous chromosomes is ncessary so that the homologous chromosomes are not inherited independently but allowing for one to go to each daughter cell in the first meiotic division. The second change is that during anaphase/telophase, the kinetochores attach and pull homologous chromosomes apart to different poles instead of pulling sister chromatids apart. So the kinetochore attachment had to change orientiation along with orientation of sister chromatids to enable each chromosome to go to a different pole in meiosis while a copy of each goes to each pole in mitosis.
</text>

2. Why is homolog synapsis (pairing) critical during Prophase I of meiosis, but completely absent during mitotic prophase?

<text style="background-color:lightcyan">
Ensures Reduction Division ($2n \rightarrow n$): Synapsis physically connects homologous chromosomes via the synaptonemal complex, forming bivalents (tetrads). Crossing over creates chiasmata—physical crossover points that keep homologous pairs linked. This linkage forces homologous chromosomes to orient toward opposite spindle poles during Metaphase I, ensuring that whole homologous chromosomes segregate away from each other during Anaphase I to reduce ploidy.</text>

<text style="background-color:lightcyan">
Generates Genetic Recombination: Physical pairing brings non-sister chromatids into close alignment, allowing controlled DNA exchange that breaks linkage groups and creates novel combinations of parental alleles.</text>

3. Consider the potential evolutionary trade-offs of haploid-dominant vs. diploid-dominant life cycles:

    a. What could be one advantage of spending most of a life cycle in the haploid (n) state regarding exposure to natural selection?<br>
<text style="background-color:lightcyan">
Direct expression and immediate purging/selection. Because haploid organisms possess only a single copy of each gene, there are no dominant alleles to mask recessive alleles. Every allele in the genome is directly expressed in the phenotype. This allows natural selection to act immediately: deleterious mutations are efficiently identified and purged from the gene pool, while beneficial mutations provide an immediate fitness advantage without needing to reach homozygosity.
</text><br><br>
    b. What could be one advantage of spending most of a life cycle in the diploid (2n) state regarding harmful recessive mutations?<br>
    <text style="background-color:lightcyan">    
Genetic masking (buffering). Diploid organisms carry two copies of every chromosome. If a harmful recessive mutation occurs on one chromosome, its expression is typically masked by a functional, wild-type allele on the homologous chromosome. This shields the organism from the immediate fitness cost of deleterious mutations, allowing diploid individuals to survive and populations to accumulate genetic variation over generations.
</text><br>

4. From the list below, identify which of the following stages of the fly life cycle are haploid and which are diploid. Additionally, tell me whether the cells are produced using mitosis or meiosis.

    a. wing cells in an adult fly
    b. unfertilized eggs in a female fly
    c. a newly fertilized fly egg
    d. a young (2nd instar) fly larva body cell
    e. the epidermal cells inside a fly pupa before it hatches into an adult
    f. sperm cells in a male fly's reproductive tract<br><br>

<text style="background-color:lightcyan">
haploid, meiosis: b, f<br>
diploid, mitosis: a, c, d, e<br>
</text>

5. Among the related readings are a couple of chapters from Gathering Moss (The Advantages of Being Small and Back to the Pond). In Back to the Pond, Kimmerer talks about the moss life cycle, which is different from that of vascular plants and allows it to adapt to different conditions. Check out the graphic of a moss life cycle from Biology 2e ([link](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/25-3-bryophytes)). <b>Describe two ways in which mosses are adapted to their specific environments, compared to larger plants or other organisms.</b>

<text style="background-color:lightcyan">
Various answers are possible. Some examples:</text>

* <text style="background-color:lightcyan">boundary layer micro-climates and dessication tolerance: Because mosses lack vascular tissue (xylem and phloem) and true roots, they remain low to the ground to inhabit the "boundary layer"—a thin zone of still air directly adjacent to soil, rocks, or bark. Living in this micro-environment insulates them from wind-driven evaporation. Furthermore, mosses are poikilohydric; they can dry out completely during droughts, enter metabolic dormancy, and instantly rehydrate upon contact with water, whereas larger vascular plants require continuous root-to-leaf water transport to avoid tissue death.</text>

* <text style="background-color:lightcyan">Biphasic Life Cycle Matched to Fluid Dynamics: Mosses use different physical mediums for reproduction and dispersal depending on their developmental phase. The ground-level gametophyte relies on liquid water films (or splashing raindrops) for flagellated sperm to swim to the egg. Following fertilization, the diploid sporophyte grows an elevated stalk and capsule extending upward above the stagnant boundary layer into moving air currents, enabling wind to carry lightweight haploid spores across long distances to colonize distant micro-habitats.
</text>
